examples: The night view from here is just like a dream.
He was as happy as a child.
The clouds look just like cotton.
He kept talking as if nothing had happened.
It's all technical terms, so I don't understand it at all.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a vivid, emotional comparison; suited to descriptive writing.
With ～かのようだ: a nuance of "as if", avoiding a claim about reality.
With ～ない: means "not at all", close to まったく/ぜんぜん, but まるで feels more strongly emphatic in written language.
ようだ vs みたいだ: ようだ is formal/written; みたいだ is casual/spoken.

まるで emphasizes a degree of resemblance or strangeness to the point of "just like, exactly like". With ようだ/みたいだ it forms a figurative comparison; with ～ない it means "not at all". かのようだ adds a hypothetical nuance and is written language.
• まるで + N のようだ: describes the whole as "exactly like N".
• まるで + ように/ような: modifies manner/quality.
• まるで + みたい: colloquial, casual, very frequent in conversation.
fields.notes:
• The negative structure "まるで～ない" is often used when feeling "helpless / not understanding / having nothing", with a stronger nuance than ぜんぜん in written language.
• For concrete images, まるで + N みたい is the natural choice in everyday conversation.
• Avoid overusing it in formal writing: choose ようだ/かのようだ for balance.
mistakes: Using まるで in the affirmative without ようだ/みたいだ: ×まるで綺麗 → 〇まるで綺麗な絵のようだ.
Confusing まるで～ない with まったく～ない: both mean "not at all", but まるで often goes with できない/分からない in emphatic writing.
Confusing formality: みたいだ is colloquial and unsuitable for academic writing; use ようだ/かのようだ.

fields.connection: もしも + N/Naなら / もしも + V/A plain form + (の)なら
examples: If it rains tomorrow, the field trip will be canceled.
If you have time, please read this document.
If he doesn't come, I'll go.
If I were a bird, I would want to fly freely in the sky.
If you can't make it in time, please start first.
If it's dangerous, let's give up that plan.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize "supposing" or "in the worst case".
Suited to warnings, safety instructions and contingency plans: もしも火事 なら、非常口へ。
Creates a polite/gentle feel when asking: もしもご都合が悪い なら、日程を変えます。
Combines flexibly with ～たら／～場合は to express a specific point in time or situation.

• "もしも～なら": If by chance / supposing / if ... then ...; emphasizes supposition, usually an unlikely situation or a contingency scenario.
• More formal in nuance than "もし～なら", with a feel of "if something should happen" or "a strong hypothesis".
• Often used to set a condition before giving advice, an option, or a counter-question.
• Compared with ～たら: なら focuses on a condition that has been stated/is known, while たら suggests the time when the condition actually occurs.
fields.notes:
• "もしも" often appears in guide titles: もしもの時に備える (preparing for emergencies).
• "なら" suits conditions given by or known to the listener; easy to use in interactive conversation.
• In emotional writing, "もしも～なら" opens up imagination: もしも生まれ変われるなら… | Variants: もしも～たら・もしもの場合
mistakes: Confusing "なら" with the time relation of "たら": contingency plans use なら/場合は; events in actual sequence use たら.
Forgetting that "もしも" only adds emphasis and does not change the verb/adjective conjugation: still use 普通形 + なら.
Using "と" with volition/commands is wrong: もしも地震が起こると、逃げてください（wrong） → 起こったら／起こるなら（correct in context).

rows: More neutral; "もしも" is more emphatic.
もし<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して。
Tied to the time something actually happens.

Not compatible with volition; leans toward general rules.

Concession; the result does not change.

examples: If he had come, I could have talked to him directly.
If I had studied harder back then, I might have passed.
If we had left earlier, we probably wouldn't have gotten caught in traffic.
If you had told the truth, there would have been no misunderstanding.
If she had been a doctor, she could have saved them.
If I had been watching carefully, I could have noticed the mistake.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes the counterfactual nature of the condition; suited to expressing regret / "if only".
The second clause often comes with のに／だろう／よかった to express emotion and inference.
Spoken language often simplifies it to もし～たら; use ～たなら when you want to emphasize "the condition did not happen".
Avoid using it for real conditions in the present/future (use もし～たら／～なら／～ば instead).

• Counterfactual supposition about the past: "If ... had ... (but in reality it didn't), then ...".
• Often expresses regret or infers a result that could have happened.
• The second clause often uses のに／だろう／よかった（のに）／と思う／かもしれない to show the hypothetical consequence.
• Unlike もし～たら (neutral), ～たなら emphasizes that "the condition did not happen".
fields.notes:
• Inversion can be used to emphasize the result first: 会えたのに、もし彼が来ていたなら。 (written language).
• ～ていたなら emphasizes a state continuing at a past point in time: 雨がやんでいたなら…
• "もしも" strengthens the hypothetical/remote nuance, often used in warnings/scenarios: もしも地震が起きていたなら… explain: Used to put forward a hypothesis about something that is not real and the consequence of that unreal thing ⏐ examples: 1. もし試験を受けていたなら、合格していたと思う。
If I had taken the exam, I think I would have passed
2. もし彼が社長でなかったなら、会社はつぶれていたと思う。
If he hadn't been the president, I think the company would have gone under
3. もし、留学しなかったなら、今ごろは国で結婚しているだろう。
If I hadn't studied abroad, I would probably be married in my home country by now
mistakes: Using it for the future: × もし明日雨が降ったなら、行かない → use もし明日雨が降ったら/降れば.
Not using the past in the conditional clause: × もし行くなら会えたのに → ✓ もし行ったなら会えたのに.
Confusing it with ～ばよかった: ～たなら needs two clauses; ～ばよかった expresses regret on its own.
JLPT: pay attention to the counterfactual nuance and the endings のに／だろう／よかった to choose the correct answer.

fields.connection: 必ずしも + V/A plain form + とは限らない
examples: Just because something is expensive doesn't necessarily mean it's good quality.
Studying abroad doesn't necessarily mean your Japanese will improve.
Rumors aren't necessarily true.
People who work fast don't necessarily make fewer mistakes.
The reason more data isn't always better is that quality matters more than quantity.
fields.explain:
A cautious, counterargument nuance; neutral to slightly formal, usable in reports and discussions.
Often appears with: ～からといって,一般的に…が、必ずしも…,見た目は…が、必ずしも…
Not used for a definitive 100% negation; implies "it depends on the case".
Position: usually in the middle of the sentence; putting 必ずしも…とは限らない at the beginning of a sentence is also natural in writing.

• "Not necessarily / not always ...": negates a general statement.
• Emphasizes the existence of exceptions or that the degree is not absolute. 必ずしも strengthens the meaning "not absolute".
• Usually follows a general judgment, preconception or conjecture in order to argue against it.
• Logically it is a "negation of necessity", not total negation (it does not say it is completely wrong).
fields.notes:
• In casual speech it can be slightly shortened into a contracted form: とは限らない → とは限んない (colloquial).
• Avoid using it with commands/requests; this is a pattern of evaluation, not a request for action.
• Scope negation: 必ずしもAではない differs from "Aは全くない"; do not translate it as "not at all". meaning_vi: Not certain that / not necessarily / not limited to ⏐ explain: Usually used to negate a proposition, saying that a situation does not apply to everything, not to all cases ⏐ examples: 1. （お）金持ちが必ずしも幸福だとは限らない。
Being rich doesn't necessarily mean being happy
2. 高いものが必ずいいものだとは限らない。
Expensive things aren't necessarily good things
mistakes: Confusing it with "not at all": 必ずしもAではない ≠ 全くAではない.
Dropping 必ずしも: using ～とは限らない on its own is still correct, but exam questions often require it together for emphasis.
Confusing the direction of meaning with ～ないとは限らない (reversed meaning). Read the position of ない carefully.
Polite form: とは限りません, not とは限られません.

examples: I will never give up.
This is by no means your fault.
Please never tell anyone the secret.
Prices in Japan are by no means cheap.
It's not that I doubt him at all, but it still needs to be confirmed.
fields.explain:
Used for prohibition, warnings and strong commitments: signs, rules, promises.
"は" in安く は ない creates a contrastive nuance and emphasizes the negative.
Suited to formal written language; in everyday conversation it can sound somewhat harsh.

• "Absolutely not / by no means / never ...".
• Emphasizes will, rules or strong evaluation; a stiff, decisive nuance.
• Can express an oath/promise: 決して忘れない (I will never forget).
• Unlike "not necessarily": 決して expresses strong negation, not partial negation.
fields.notes:
• Natural combinations: 決して～してはいけない／忘れてはならない／油断してはならない.
• In strong statements, it often comes at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis: 決して～ない。
• Avoid using it with vague judgments; 決して requires a clear position. meaning_vi: Absolutely not, definitely not, never ⏐ explain: Used to show determination not to do something ⏐ examples: 1. 私は決して夢をあきらめません。
I will never give up on my dream
2. 「うそは決して申しません。」と彼は言った。
He said, "I will never tell a lie"
mistakes: Forgetting the negative after 決して: wrong "決して行く" → correct "決して行かない/行きません".
Confusing it with 必ず (definitely): 決して = absolutely not, 必ず = definitely (affirmative).
Overusing it in casual conversation makes the sentence sound harsh.
Distinguish its degree from 全然/絶対に: exam questions often ask about nuance.

fields.name: Contracted form（～ている／～でいる）
fields.meaning:
Contracted form: ～ている → てる／～でいる → でる
Contracted form: ～ておく → とく／～でおく → どく
Contracted form: ～なければ → なきゃ
Contracted form: ～なくては/～なければ → なくちゃ/なきゃ
fields.connection: Vている → Vてる / Vでいる → Vでる（spoken contraction）
examples: "Who's that person sitting over there?"
"I'll be right there, so go on ahead."
"What's wrong? If you just cry, I won't understand. You have to tell me why."
"Please read this book by next week."
"Where should I put this away?" "You can just leave it on the desk."
"Please make a note of the important things."
fields.explain:
Casual contracted form of ～ている／～でいる, commonly used in everyday conversation.
Casual contracted form of ～ておく／～でおく, still keeping the meaning of doing something in advance or preparing.
Casual contracted form of ～なければ, often used in conversation.
Casual contracted form of the obligation patterns "must…", used a lot in spoken language.
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse the contracted form with the standard form in written language.
→ てる／でる is colloquial, mainly used in conversation.
2) On the JLPT, pay attention to spoken-language contexts.
→ Choose the contracted form only if the sentence has a casual, quick, conversational nuance.
3) Not used in formal documents, announcements or essays.
→ Written language usually uses ～ている／～でいる.

fields.name: Expressions using intransitive verbs
fields.connection: Nが/は + V intransitive verb（describing property・function: 入る・開く）
examples: This bag is light and holds a lot, so it's convenient for traveling.
This manga is selling well. It must be popular.
"It's fragile, so please carry it carefully."
My hair doesn't take a perm easily.
This kitchen knife cuts well.
fields.explain: Uses an intransitive verb to express a property, state or ability as a natural condition, without emphasizing the agent.
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse intransitive verbs with transitive verbs.
→ This pattern uses intransitive verbs to talk about a property/state (ability, characteristics), without emphasizing the agent who does it.
2) Often used with words meaning "easy/hard" or describing properties.
→ For example: 開きやすい, 壊れやすい… usually properties of things.
3) When there is a clear agent, a transitive verb or another structure is usually used.
→ If you want to say "someone does…", do not use this intransitive-verb style describing a state.

fields.meaning:
Expresses a reason. Used to say "... is because of ..."
［ふつう］　+　からだ
examples: It's because I thought it wasn't good.
I overslept again. It must be because I'm tired. (≒ I overslept because I'm tired)
The reason I overslept is that I'm tired. (≒ I overslept because I'm tired)

The traffic is probably this bad because there was some kind of accident.
(≒ Because there was some kind of accident, traffic is this backed up)
fields.notes:
This form is the reason pattern "X から Y" inverted into "Y のは X からだ". The から in this pattern cannot be replaced with ので.
* (incorrect) 試験に落ちたのは勉強しなかったのでだ。

fields.name: （imperative form）と頼まれる
examples: I was asked to tell (them)
Mr. Yamashita asked me to give him Mr. Tanaka's email address.
When I told my mother I wanted to study in Japan, she told me not to go.

fields.name: （imperative form）と言われる
fields.connection: 「V imperative form / Vるな」 + と言われる
examples: To be told not to go
My father told me to come back home during summer vacation.
My teacher warned me not to be late.
Whenever I go back to my home country, my mother always tells me, "Eat more."
That's all for self-introductions. Now, let's get to the main topic.
We've finished reviewing last lesson. Now, let's move on to new grammar.
Sorry to have kept you waiting so long. Now, I'll announce the results.
That completes the preparations. Now, let's set off.
Now, here's a question. Which of the following is correct?
fields.explain:
Polite, inviting nuance that guides the listener; often used in presentations, classes and emails.
Position: at the beginning of a sentence/new clause; followed by a comma.
Used to "change direction" or "move forward", not to comment or give an evaluation.
Not used to change abruptly to an unrelated topic (use ところで in that case).
In emails: " さて、早速ですが…" to move on to the main content.

さて: "well/now then/so now…", used to:
• Move on to the next topic or return to the main topic after an introduction.
• Move to the next step in a procedure/instruction/explanation.
• Start a new action and draw the listener's attention.
• Does not express cause-and-effect or same-direction addition; purely a transition.
fields.notes:
• In spoken language, the intonation often rises slightly after "さて" to draw attention.
• "さてさて" can be repeated in casual spoken language to soften the atmosphere.
• In formal language, "それでは/では" is usually safer when announcing a decision/action. explain: Used when changing to a new topic. ⏐ examples: 1. 「これで授業を終わります。さて来週の予定ですが・・・」
This is the end of the class. Now, about next week's schedule…
2. 「以上、今日のニュースをお伝えしました。さて次に天気予報です。」
That's all for today's news. And now, the weather forecast.
mistakes: Confusing it with ところで: exam questions often test the context; if the two sentences are connected/move forward a step → さて; if the topic changes abruptly → ところで.
Using さて for a cause-and-effect relation is wrong: use それで/したがって.
A harsh command after さて sounds forced; use an inviting form instead.
